questions.question: State the Big Bang theory and the Hubble law. What evidence supports the expanding universe?
questions.solution:
**Big Bang theory:** The universe began as an extremely hot, dense point ~13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.

**Hubble's law:** v = H₀d — galaxies recede from us at velocities proportional to their distance. H₀ ≈ 67-70 km/s/Mpc.

**Evidence:**
1. Redshift of distant galaxies (Doppler shift)
2. Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) at 2.7 K
3. Abundance of light elements (H, He) matches Big Bang predictions
questions.knowledgeNote: Hubble's discovery (1929) showed that most galaxies are redshifted, meaning they are moving away — the universe is expanding.
questions.answer: **Big Bang theory:** the universe began about **13.8 billion years ago** from an extremely hot, dense state and has been **expanding and cooling ever since**; the early universe was radiation-dominated, forming the light nuclei (H, He) in the first minutes (nucleosynthesis) and becoming transparent ~380 000 years in (recombination, releasing the cosmic microwave background). **Hubble's law:** galaxies recede with velocity proportional to their distance — **v = H₀d** (H₀ ≈ 70 km/s per megaparsec); observed as the **redshift** of galactic spectra, and interpreted as the stretching of space itself, not galaxies flying through space. **Evidence for the expanding universe:** (1) **Hubble's redshift–distance law** — the recession velocity of galaxies grows linearly with distance; (2) the **cosmic microwave background (CMB)** — the cooled (~2.7 K) relic radiation of the hot early universe, matching the prediction of a fireball phase; (3) the **abundance of light elements** (≈75% H, 25% He by mass) matching Big Bang nucleosynthesis calculations; (4) the large-scale distribution and evolution of galaxies consistent with gradual structure formation from a hot uniform start. **Deep point:** the three independent lines — redshifts, CMB, light-element abundances — converge on the same early-universe parameters; a static or steady-state universe predicts none of them, which is why the evidence is considered decisive.
